newsitem.title: FRANCE: OECD says French corporate system hurts profits.
newsitem.headline: OECD says French corporate system hurts profits.

text.p: The French system of corporate governance hurts profitability and leads to lower return on equity than that generated in systems with freer control of capital, the OECD said in a report issued on Thursday.
It said France's biggest listed companies had an average return on own equity (ROE) of 8.5 percent between 1993 and 1995.

While this puts France ahead of Japan's 4.8 percent rate, it trails Germany, the United States and Britain. Their ROE is 10.5, 18 and 18.5 percent, respectively, over the same period, the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development said.
The more typical of the French system a company is, the lower its profitability, the OECD said.

"During the 1991-95 period, moreover, public companies and companies privatised since 1986 (ie those most characteristic of corporate governance a la francaise) had the lowest rates of ROE and the lowest price to book ratios," the OECD report said.

It cited Elf Aquitaine, privatised in 1993 with a ROE of 5.7 percent during the 1991-95 period, Banque Nationale de Paris with a ROE of 4.3 percent over the same time and Paribas, with a ROE of 0.1 percent.

The French system is characterised by cross-shareholdings which shield "managers from the short-term pressures of the market by making a change in corporate control more difficult -- a feature that may be conducive to long-term, relation-specific investments, but one that also weakens pressures to maximise performance," it said.

The development of the French-style system partly reflects a dearth of pension capital in the equities market and a drive to protect newly listed companies from unsolicited bids by establishing a "hard core" of long-term stable shareholders.

The OECD welcomed proposals in France to establish private pension funds. "If funds would rise to a certain importance -- this is not certain, as pension coverage by the pay-as-you-go system is high -- and if funds were independent from listed companies and their shareholders, the new funds would contribute to changing the corporate governance landscape," it said.
The OECD report said the level of venture capital in France was "relatively important", and it ranked France in second place behind the United States among OECD countries.

But it said less money was allocated to startup -- or seed -- capital in France than elsewhere. A recent French study showed startup capital accounted for only six percent of total venture capital, compared with 13.5 percent in the United States.

The report said the creation by the Paris stockmarket of the small capitalisation Nouveau Marche and the increased number of listings on the U.S. NASDAQ should boost financing for small and mid-sized companies in the future since investors should be able to sell their holdings and realise capital gains.
